stem: A client with cirrhotic ascites is following a sodium-restricted diet but is now eating very little and losing muscle mass because the food is unpalatable. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Assess the client's nutritional status and collaborate with the dietitian and treating team; if sodium restriction is preventing adequate intake, consider an individualized adjustment of the restriction.
options.B: Maintain the current sodium restriction unchanged and focus on ascites control first, postponing nutrition-plan changes until weight and muscle loss become more pronounced.
options.C: Further reduce dietary sodium and lower protein intake at the same time so fluid retention decreases more quickly while the client adapts to the restricted diet.
options.D: Continue the current sodium restriction and add extra fasting periods between meals so the client can reduce total intake without changing the prescribed diet.

rationale: AASLD guidance recognizes malnutrition and sarcopenia as clinically important complications of cirrhosis and states that sodium restriction can reduce food palatability and become a barrier to adequate oral intake. AASLD advises that liberalization of sodium restriction should be considered when a client cannot maintain nutritional targets and emphasizes individualized nutrition counseling. Therefore A is correct and preserves the source's conditional language rather than making liberalization automatic. B delays response to active nutritional deterioration. C compounds poor intake by adding further sodium and protein restriction; AASLD specifically advises against protein restriction in cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy and emphasizes adequate protein intake generally. D adds prolonged fasting, which AASLD recommends minimizing because of catabolic risk.
educational_objective: When sodium restriction in cirrhosis is contributing to poor intake and muscle loss, reassess nutritional status and collaborate on an individualized diet; consider relaxing the restriction when needed to meet nutritional targets rather than intensifying restriction or delaying intervention.
source_organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
source_document_title: Back to Basics: Outpatient Management of Cirrhosis; Malnutrition in the Adult with Cirrhosis
source_version_date: Outpatient-management resource published February 15, 2024 and current on the AASLD site in 2026; malnutrition clinical resource current on the AASLD site in 2026
source_locator: Back to Basics: Outpatient Management of Cirrhosis > Malnutrition in Cirrhosis: sodium restriction can decrease food palatability and create a barrier to adequate oral intake; liberalization of sodium restriction should be considered in patients who are malnourished on a sodium-restricted diet. Malnutrition in the Adult with Cirrhosis > Intake Interventions — Macronutrients: liberalization of sodium restriction should be considered if a patient is unable to maintain nutritional targets; protein intake should not be restricted in hepatic encephalopathy; fasting time should be minimized. > Take Home Points: engage at-risk patients in team-based nutrition counseling and individualize dietary counseling regarding salt, protein, and other interventions.
source_claim_supported: AASLD directly supports active nutritional assessment and individualized dietary management in cirrhosis, including considering liberalization of sodium restriction when poor palatability or restriction prevents adequate intake and contributes to malnutrition.

supporting_sources.organization: American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD)
supporting_sources.document_title: Malnutrition in the Adult with Cirrhosis
supporting_sources.locator: Intake Interventions — Macronutrients: consider liberalizing sodium restriction when nutritional targets cannot be maintained; avoid protein restriction in hepatic encephalopathy; minimize fasting. Take Home Points: use team-based and individualized nutrition counseling.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Dietary restriction should be individualized when it undermines nutritional targets, and malnutrition requires active team-based intervention.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Basic Care and Comfort > Nutrition and Oral Hydration, printed p. 37: consider client choices regarding nutritional requirements and dietary restrictions; evaluate nutritional status and intervene as needed; provide and maintain special diets based on diagnosis/nutritional needs; provide nutritional supplements as needed; evaluate the impact of disease/illness on nutritional status.
blueprint_topic: Basic Care and Comfort — individualized dietary support when sodium restriction contributes to malnutrition in cirrhosis
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four actions to remove the uniquely-long keyed answer and preserve AASLD's conditional language: sodium liberalization is considered when restriction prevents adequate intake, not automatically prescribed. Distractors now test delay, overrestriction, and prolonged fasting rather than obvious nonsense.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Cirrhosis with ascites — malnutrition caused or worsened by restrictive diet
audit_findings.stem: PASS — establishes active poor intake and muscle loss attributable to diet palatability, creating a clear nutritional reassessment problem without assuming a fixed sodium target.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly follows AASLD guidance to assess nutrition, individualize counseling, and consider relaxing sodium restriction when nutritional targets cannot be met; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — ascites control matters, but active malnutrition and muscle loss should not be allowed to progress before the nutrition plan is reassessed.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — additional restriction may appear to favor fluid control, but it worsens the stated intake problem and adds a protein restriction unsupported by current AASLD nutrition guidance.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — maintaining the current diet may appear conservative, but adding fasting directly conflicts with AASLD guidance to minimize prolonged fasting in cirrhosis.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that balances ascites management with current nutritional deterioration using the source's individualized conditional approach.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B delays intervention, C intensifies harmful restriction, and D adds catabolic fasting.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — choices are comparable in length and complexity and the keyed answer is no longer uniquely signaled by markedly greater detail.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Basic Care and Comfort directly includes nutritional-status evaluation, intervention, dietary restrictions, and diagnosis-based special diets.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether sodium restriction should remain unchanged because ascites is present; AASLD explicitly states restriction must be balanced against malnutrition and that liberalization should be considered when nutritional targets cannot be maintained, leaving A uniquely best without converting 'consider' into an automatic requirement.
